title: Local Excitation, Global Inhibition
markdown: ## What this covers How can a chemical system that is perfectly stable when stirred uniformly become unstable the moment it is allowed to diffuse, and settle instead into a fixed spatial pattern? This chapter works through one concrete answer — the Gierer–Meinhardt activator–inhibitor kinetics, a specific case of Turing's reaction–diffusion mechanism — and derives exactly when that happens. It assumes comfort with reaction–diffusion PDEs, linearizing about a steady state, and the trace/determinant test for the stability of a $2\times 2$ linear system. ## The activator–inhibitor kinetics Take two diffusing chemical species on a line: an **activator** $a(x,t)$ and an **inhibitor** $i(x,t)$. Their dynamics are $$\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial a}{\partial t} &= r_a + k_a\frac{a^2}{i} - \gamma_a a + D_a\frac{\partial^2 a}{\partial x^2} \\ \frac{\partial i}{\partial t} &= k_i a^2 - \gamma_i i + D_i\frac{\partial^2 i}{\partial x^2} \end{aligned}$$ with $r_a$ a basal (activator-independent) synthesis rate, $k_a,k_i$ rate constants, $\gamma_a,\gamma_i$ decay rates, and $D_a,D_i$ diffusion constants. This is a **Turing–Gierer–Meinhardt model**: a particular choice of reaction kinetics inside the general two-species reaction–diffusion template Turing studied. The shape of the kinetics is the whole content of the model. The activator makes more of itself — the $k_a a^2/i$ term is autocatalytic — but that autocatalysis is throttled by however much inhibitor is around, since $i$ sits in the denominator. The inhibitor, in turn, is switched on by the activator ($k_i a^2$) and simply decays on its own; it has no autocatalytic loop of its own. So the circuit is: activator turns on both itself and its own suppressor, and the suppressor turns the activator back down. Whether that circuit produces a spatial pattern, and not just a decaying disturbance, turns out to hinge entirely on how far the inhibitor's influence reaches compared to the activator's — the question the chapter title names. ## Removing the parameters: the dimensionless system and its uniform state Six dimensional constants ($r_a,k_a,k_i,\gamma_a,\gamma_i,D_a,D_i$ — the diffusion constants come in as a ratio) is more than the qualitative behaviour of the system actually depends on. Rescaling the four quantities $a,i,t,x$ against natural units built from these constants absorbs four of the parameters and leaves three dimensionless groups, $R$, $Q$, $P$. In the rescaled variables $A,I,\tau,s$: $$\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial A}{\partial \tau} &= 1 + R\frac{A^2}{I} - A + \frac{\partial^2 A}{\partial s^2} \\ \frac{\partial I}{\partial \tau} &= Q(A^2 - I) + P\frac{\partial^2 I}{\partial s^2} \end{aligned}$$ The activator's diffusion coefficient has been scaled to $1$; $P$ is what remains of the inhibitor's diffusion constant relative to it, so $P$ is a direct measure of how much faster (or slower) the inhibitor spreads than the activator. Write the reaction parts as $f(A,I)=1+RA^2/I-A$ and $g(A,I)=Q(A^2-I)$, so the system is $\partial_\tau A = f + \partial_s^2A$, $\partial_\tau I = g + P\partial_s^2 I$. The **homogeneous solution** is the spatially uniform, time-independent state: set $\partial/\partial s = \partial/\partial \tau = 0$, i.e. solve $f(\bar A,\bar I)=0$, $g(\bar A,\bar I)=0$. The second equation gives $\bar I = \bar A^2$ directly. Substituting into the first, $$1 + R\frac{\bar A^2}{\bar A^2} - \bar A = 1 + R - \bar A = 0,$$ so $$\bar A = R+1, \qquad \bar I = (R+1)^2.$$ This is the candidate pattern-free state: activator and inhibitor sitting at a fixed level everywhere in space, for all time. The question is whether it is actually reached and held, or whether the smallest disturbance grows. ## Is the uniform state stable on its own? First ask the easier question: if $(\bar A,\bar I)$ is nudged by a small amount that is the *same everywhere in space* — no spatial structure at all — does it relax back? A spatially uniform disturbance has zero second derivative in $s$, so the diffusion terms simply drop out and the question is answered entirely by the local reaction kinetics, treated as an ordinary two-variable dynamical system. Linearizing $f,g$ about $(\bar A,\bar I)$ gives the Jacobian $$J = \begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial A} & \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial I} \\[4pt] \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial A} & \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial I} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{2RA}{I}-1 & -\dfrac{RA^2}{I^2} \\[4pt] 2QA & -Q \end{pmatrix}.$$ Evaluating at $\bar A = R+1$, $\bar I=(R+1)^2$: $$\frac{\partial f}{\partial A}\Big|_{\bar A,\bar I} = \frac{2R(R+1)}{(R+1)^2}-1 = \frac{2R}{R+1}-1 = \frac{R-1}{R+1}, \qquad \frac{\partial f}{\partial I}\Big|_{\bar A,\bar I} = -\frac{R(R+1)^2}{(R+1)^4} = -\frac{R}{(R+1)^2},$$ $$\frac{\partial g}{\partial A}\Big|_{\bar A,\bar I} = 2Q(R+1), \qquad \frac{\partial g}{\partial I}\Big|_{\bar A,\bar I} = -Q,$$ so $$J = \begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{R-1}{R+1} & -\dfrac{R}{(R+1)^2} \\[4pt] 2(R+1)Q & -Q \end{pmatrix}.$$ A fixed point of a two-variable system is stable exactly when both eigenvalues of $J$ have negative real part, which for a $2\times 2$ matrix is equivalent to $\operatorname{tr} J<0$ and $\det J>0$. Here $$\operatorname{tr} J = \frac{R-1}{R+1} - Q, \qquad \det J = -Q\cdot\frac{R-1}{R+1} + \frac{2RQ}{R+1} = \frac{Q}{R+1}\big(2R-(R-1)\big) = Q.$$ So $\det J>0$ just says $Q>0$, and $\operatorname{tr} J<0$ says $$\boxed{Q > \frac{R-1}{R+1}} \qquad \text{(homogeneous stability).}$$ If this holds, a uniform disturbance to $(\bar A,\bar I)$ decays: stir the system out of equilibrium everywhere at once, and it settles right back to the same flat state. ## Turning on diffusion: does a *spatial* disturbance stay flat? Uniform stability is not the end of the story, because diffusion only acts on disturbances that vary in space — a perfectly flat perturbation never feels it. So write the perturbed state as $$A(s,\tau) = \bar A + A'(s,\tau), \qquad I(s,\tau) = \bar I + I'(s,\tau),$$ substitute into the full PDE, and keep only the linear terms in $A',I'$. The reaction part gives back exactly the Jacobian entries found above; the diffusion terms survive this time because $A',I'$ are allowed to depend on $s$: $$\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial A'}{\partial \tau} &= \frac{R-1}{R+1}A' - \frac{R}{(R+1)^2}I' + \frac{\partial^2 A'}{\partial s^2} \\ \frac{\partial I'}{\partial \tau} &= 2Q(R+1)A' - QI' + P\frac{\partial^2 I'}{\partial s^2} \end{aligned}$$ To see how a disturbance with a definite spatial scale behaves, try a single spatial Fourier mode — a disturbance that oscillates in space with "wavelength" set by $\ell$, and whose *amplitude* $\hat A,\hat I$ is free to grow or decay in time: $$A'(s,\tau) = \hat A(\tau)\cos\!\left(\frac{s}{\ell}\right), \qquad I'(s,\tau) = \hat I(\tau)\cos\!\left(\frac{s}{\ell}\right).$$ Since $\partial_s^2\cos(s/\ell) = -\ell^{-2}\cos(s/\ell)$, each diffusion term just multiplies the amplitude by $-1/\ell^2$ (for $A'$) or $-P/\ell^2$ (for $I'$), and the system collapses to an ordinary pair of ODEs for the amplitudes: $$\begin{aligned} \frac{d\hat A}{d\tau} &= \left(\frac{R-1}{R+1} - \frac{1}{\ell^2}\right)\hat A - \frac{R}{(R+1)^2}\hat I \\ \frac{d\hat I}{d\tau} &= 2Q(R+1)\hat A - \left(Q+\frac{P}{\ell^2}\right)\hat I \end{aligned}$$ This is the same trace/determinant question as before, but now for a new matrix $J_\ell$ that is $J$ with $1/\ell^2$ subtracted from the top-left entry and $P/\ell^2$ subtracted from the bottom-right — diffusion simply damps each species at a rate that grows with the mode's spatial frequency $1/\ell$. Write $x = 1/\ell^2 \ge 0$ and, for brevity, $\alpha = (R-1)/(R+1)$ for the diagonal reaction entry found above. Then $$\operatorname{tr} J_\ell = (\alpha - Q) - (1+P)x, \qquad \det J_\ell = Px^2 + (Q-\alpha P)x + Q.$$ If the homogeneous condition $Q>\alpha$ already holds, $\operatorname{tr}J_\ell$ only gets more negative as $x$ increases, so the trace condition is never the one that can fail here — spatial modes are only ever threatened through $\det J_\ell$. As a quadratic in $x\ge 0$ opening upward (since $P>0$) and equal to $Q>0$ at $x=0$, $\det J_\ell$ stays positive for **every** wavenumber exactly when its vertex lies at $x\le 0$, i.e. when the coefficient $Q-\alpha P$ is non-negative: $$\boxed{\frac{Q}{P} > \frac{R-1}{R+1}} \qquad \text{(inhomogeneous stability).}$$ When this holds, $\det J_\ell>0$ for every spatial mode, so *no* pattern of any wavelength grows: a spatially varying disturbance $I'$ relaxes back to $\bar I$ just as a uniform one does. When it fails — when $Q/P$ drops below $(R-1)/(R+1)$ — the vertex of the parabola moves to positive $x$, and $\det J_\ell$ can dip below zero for a band of intermediate wavenumbers: those modes grow, and the flat state gives way to a spatial pattern. ## When patterning wins: local excitation, global inhibition Now put the two boxed conditions side by side: $$\text{homogeneous stability:}\quad Q > \frac{R-1}{R+1}, \qquad\qquad \text{inhomogeneous stability:}\quad \frac{Q}{P} > \frac{R-1}{R+1}.$$ A genuine Turing instability — a system that is stable when disturbed uniformly but breaks into a pattern when disturbed with spatial structure — needs the first to hold and the second to fail: $$\frac{R-1}{R+1} < Q < P\cdot\frac{R-1}{R+1}.$$ For this window to exist at all (with $(R-1)/(R+1)>0$, i.e. $R>1$), it forces $$P > 1,$$ that is, $D_i > D_a$: the inhibitor must diffuse **faster** — reach farther — than the activator. That is exactly the asymmetry the chapter's name refers to. The activator's positive feedback on itself is confined to wherever the activator already is; the inhibitor it triggers spreads out past that region and suppresses activator growth everywhere nearby. A local, self-reinforcing excitation survives only inside a halo of longer-range inhibition — never in a system where both species diffuse at comparable rates. ## Sources - Slides: `01-local-excitation-global-inhibition.md` — the Turing–Gierer–Meinhardt PDE system, the nondimensionalized $A,I$ form, and the homogeneous solution $\bar A=R+1$, $\bar I=(R+1)^2$. - Slides: `02-stability-of-homogeneous-solution.md` — the Jacobian at the homogeneous state, the trace/determinant conditions for homogeneous stability, the perturbation ansatz and Fourier trial solution, the resulting amplitude equations, and the boxed homogeneous/inhomogeneous stability conditions and their qualitative reading ("relaxes back to $\bar I$"). - Both files are lecture 16 of MIT OCW 8.591J (Systems Biology, Fall 2004); both are flagged in their own headers as a model's reconstruction of a PDF slide deck with no text layer, so every displayed equation is unverified against the original scan and should be checked there before being treated as a citable statement. - No transcript, notes, or exercises were supplied for this lecture, so the intermediate algebra connecting the boxed results, the discussion of what "local excitation, global inhibition" means mechanistically, and the closing $P>1$ argument and figure are this chapter's own derivation from the slide equations, not spoken material — the lecture's oral motivation for this model is not captured in what was supplied.
